title: The Shape of Fear
sub: Grades 5–8 · Art · Silhouette, a three-color palette and what you leave out
objective: Students will read the Fear Lab’s two posters as designs. With three colors (a navy ground, cream type and marigold subheads) and a few flat silhouettes (a spider, a clawed hand, a caped vampire seen from behind), they make fear without showing a single monster’s face. Students will connect that to the science on poster 1: the brain *“sees faces and threats where none exist”* and its imagination *“creates horrors worse than reality.”* Then they will design a three-color image whose monster the viewer has to finish.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Posters, film titles and book covers all use these tricks on you. Seeing how little it takes to make a feeling lets you read them, and make your own.

items.text: name three choices that make the Fear Lab posters feel frightening: a limited palette, flat silhouettes and what is left out
items.question: name three choices that make the posters feel frightening?

items.text: explain why a shape you can’t quite see can scare you more than one you can
items.question: explain why a half-seen shape can be scarier than a clear one?

items.text: design a three-color image built on a silhouette
items.question: design a three-color image built on a silhouette?

items.text: leave the monster for the viewer to finish, and explain every choice in an artist’s statement
items.question: make the viewer finish the monster, and explain your choices?

materials: The *Show your class* page (page 3), projected or printed; the posters online if you have a screen
Dark, light and bright colors for each student (paper, paint or markers); black paper and scissors if you have them
A flashlight, if you have one; differentiated handouts, one per student
questions: What shapes did the designer use to make you feel scared? Is any of them actually a monster?
Cover the marigold with your hand. What changes?
Why show the vampire from behind?
The poster says the real terror isn’t the creature, it’s what it represents. What might a spider or a hand stand for?
questionsLabel: Questions to ask in front of the posters
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** both posters, then the walkthroughs online, which set the spider dropping and the hand rising beside the text.

steps.title: The face we never see
script: Show poster 2’s vampire, seen from behind. Ask: *“Who is he? What does his face look like?”* Let students describe it in detail. Then point out: *nobody here has seen it.* Every face they described came from their own imagination. Ask: *“Why might the artist have hidden it?”*

screen.alt: Illustration of a caped vampire in a red-lined cloak, seen from behind against a stormy, moonlit sky
screen.caption: Who is he? What does his face look like?

steps.purpose: Notice that the most frightening part of the picture is the part that isn’t there.
students: Who is he? What does his face look like?
Why might the artist have hidden it?

steps.title: A limited palette
script: **A limited palette.** Show poster 1. Both posters use the same three colors: a navy ground, cream type and marigold subheads, with black for the spider. Ask what each color does: the navy is night, the cream glows like moonlight, the marigold pulls the eye to the headings.

screen.alt: The Science of Being Scared: Fear Lab poster: the title in cream capitals on navy beside a black spider, above a box of text and a cream clawed hand reaching up
screen.caption: Navy ground, cream type, marigold subheads

steps.purpose: See how much mood three colors can make.
students: Which color does your eye go to first? Why?

steps.title: A flat shape
script: **A flat shape.** Show the clawed hand: one cream shape, no shading, no detail. Poster 1 explains why it works: *“Your brain is a pattern-seeking machine that sees faces and threats where none exist.”* *“Shadow people? Just your brain turning random darkness into human shapes.”* A silhouette gives the brain just enough to finish the rest.

screen.alt: The poster’s clawed hand: a flat cream shape with long, curved fingers
screen.caption: Shadow people? Just your brain turning random darkness into human shapes.

steps.purpose: See that a silhouette works because the brain fills it in.
students: What does your brain say this is?
What detail is missing? Do you miss it?

steps.title: Leave it out
script: **Leave it out.** Read: *“That’s why reaching into a mystery box feels scarier than touching what’s actually inside—your imagination creates horrors worse than reality.”* That is a design rule as much as a scientific one. Poster 2 adds horror’s golden rule: *the real terror isn’t the creature, it’s what it represents.*

screen.text: That’s why reaching into a mystery box feels scarier than touching what’s actually inside—your imagination creates horrors worse than reality.

steps.purpose: Turn the science into a design rule: show less, and let the viewer imagine more.
students: What would you leave out of your design?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three look closely at the posters, then make a three-color design built on a silhouette.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Name the posters’ three colors, turn a blob into a silhouette creature with nothing but eyes, then make a three-color picture of something half-seen in the dark.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Take apart poster 2’s vampire as a design, sketch three thumbnails of an everyday thing made frightening by its silhouette, then make the best one in three colors.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Compare the two posters’ choices, design a shape that is two things at once, then make a three-color poster for a fear of their own generation and write an artist’s statement.

steps.purpose: Design with a limited palette and a silhouette, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three end in a three-color design built on a silhouette.

steps.title: What did your brain fill in?
script: Lay the designs out as a gallery. Each student stands at a classmate’s work and answers: *“Look at a classmate’s design. What did your brain fill in that isn’t on the page?”* The artist listens and doesn’t explain.

screen.question: Look at a classmate’s design. What did your brain fill in that isn’t on the page?

steps.purpose: Test each design on a viewer: what did they imagine?
students: Then say what isn’t on the page at all.

steps.title: Look back
script: Then ask the objectives back as questions: *“Can you now…?”* Students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Exit ticket: *“Name one thing you left out on purpose, and why.”*

screen.hint: Show me: thumb up, sideways or down.
